# Agentic Agents {#sec-app-agents}

An agent is an assistant put in a loop: it plans, acts, observes, and tries
again. This chapter explains how the agentic pattern got the shape it has:
why the model is wrapped in a control loop, why planning and reflection
were added, and where the loop fails. By the end a reader can explain why
agents are built as loops over a model rather than as a single call.

## Problem

A single completion cannot solve a task that needs several dependent steps,
feedback from the world, or recovery from a wrong turn. The task is open
ended and the right next action depends on what the last one returned.

## Design

A perceive-plan-act loop around the model: the model chooses an action,
the system executes it, the result re-enters the context, and the loop
repeats until a stop condition. Planning and reflection structure the
choices.

## Evolution

From single tool calls, to the reason-and-act pattern (ReAct), to explicit
planning and self-reflection, to multi-agent decompositions. Trace why each
addition was forced by the failure modes of the simpler loop.

## Trade-offs

The loop adds capability and unbounded cost, latency, and error
accumulation. More autonomy means less predictability. Multi-agent setups
add parallelism and coordination overhead and new failure modes.

## In practice

Loop control and stop conditions, context and memory management across
steps, cost and latency budgets, sandboxing of actions, and evaluating a
trajectory rather than a single answer.

## Foundations

Why and when the loop helps. The agent as a policy over a partially
observed environment, planning as search, and the conditions under which
iteration and reflection provably reduce error rather than compound it.
